Case study: Two-level latent class analysis of leisure activities

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/case-esm-lca.Rmd
case-esm-lca.Rmd

Two-level latent class analysis estimates latent classes of categorical responses at the level of single observations and, above them, latent group classes that differ in how probable each class is for their observations. In the output the observation-level classes are called profiles. Each profile is described by the probability of every answer to every item; the group classes differ only in how often their observations fall in each profile.

The question here is whether the leisure activities that university students report in daily life form a small number of recurring patterns, and whether students differ in how often they are in each pattern.

Data

student_esm holds experience-sampling data from a study of university students (Neubauer & Schmiedek, 2024). The students answered six prompts a day for fourteen days. At each prompt when they had not studied since the previous one, they reported which of eight leisure activities they had done. The dataset holds these prompts for 100 students: 2,582 prompts, between 15 and 51 per student. Prompts are the observations and students the groups, so a student contributes many rows.

The eight activities are yes/no items, and they are named once so that each model can refer to them.

library(latents)
activities <- c("time_with_friends", "on_social_media", "tv_video_games",
                "listened_music", "sports", "walking", "reading",
                "part_time_job")

summary() counts the answers to each activity item and summarizes the other variables.

summary(student_esm)

Social media is the most frequent activity, reported at 745 of the 2,582 prompts, followed by TV or video games at 549. A part-time job is the rarest, at 103 prompts. Every item is answered “no” at most prompts, so a profile is described by how much more often than average its prompts say “yes”.

The model

For prompt tt of student ii, let CitC_{it} be the profile and GiG_i the student’s class. The model estimates three sets of probabilities:

  • the response probabilities θkjc=P(Yitj=c∣Cit=k)\theta_{kjc}=P(Y_{itj}=c\mid C_{it}=k) of each answer cc to item jj in profile kk, the same in every student class;
  • the profile probabilities πk∣m=P(Cit=k∣Gi=m)\pi_{k\mid m}=P(C_{it}=k\mid G_i=m) of each student class mm, which sum to one across profiles;
  • the class probabilities ωm=P(Gi=m)\omega_m=P(G_i=m).

The items are assumed independent given the profile, the prompts of a student independent given the student’s class, and the students independent of one another. The likelihood can have several local maxima, so each model is started from several random values. A rare answer can drive a response probability to its lower bound, and too many profiles or classes for the data show up as starts that fail to reach the same maximum.

How many profiles and classes

enumerate_classes() fits every combination of two to four profiles and one to three student classes, each from twenty random starts with a tight convergence tolerance, and reports the information criteria and the diagnostics of each fit. It does not choose a model.

candidates <- enumerate_classes(student_esm, vars = activities,
                                categorical = activities, id = "student",
                                n_profiles = 2:4, n_group_classes = 1:3,
                                n_starts = 20, tol = 1e-10, seed = 1)
#> 2 of 9 candidates reached their best log likelihood from one start only (classes3_groups3, classes4_groups3); refit those you consider with more starts.
as.data.frame(candidates)

The criteria disagree, and the diagnostics explain why. BIC with the number of students keeps falling up to the largest model in the grid, four profiles and three classes. That model and the one with three profiles and three classes reach their best solution from a single start (n_best_replicated), so their low BIC rests on solutions that the starts do not replicate. The criteria that also penalize classification uncertainty (ICL, AWE and CLC counted over prompts) choose three profiles and two classes, a model whose best solution recurs in 2 of the twenty starts.

The number of starts is part of the analysis on these data. With five starts and the default tolerance, the three-profile, two-class model stops at a lower maximum of the likelihood, and the same criteria then choose two profiles and two classes.

The ICL plot shows the choice across the grid.

plot_enumeration(candidates, what = "icl_individual")

The plot marks the minimum at three profiles and two classes, and the analysis continues with that model.

The chosen model

multilca() fits it, treating every item as categorical, with twenty random starts and a tight convergence tolerance, which the standard errors below need.

lca <- multilca(student_esm, vars = activities, id = "student",
                n_profiles = 3, n_group_classes = 2, n_starts = 20,
                tol = 1e-10, seed = 1)
get_results(lca, "model")
#>   n_observations n_informative n_groups n_profiles n_group_classes centering scaling
#> 1           2582          2582      100          3               2      none    none
#>   covariance_structure n_parameters n_parameters_with_measurement log_likelihood   aic bic_groups
#> 1                  VVI           29                            29          -7678 15414      15490
#>   bic_individual converged iterations boundary small_classes best_start n_best_replicated weights
#> 1          15584      TRUE         81    FALSE         FALSE         16                 2    <NA>

The fit converges, and 2 of the twenty starts reach the best log likelihood of -7678.

Three activity profiles

The "responses" table gives the probability of each answer in each profile, with a “no” and a “yes” row for every item. The “yes” rows carry the information, since the two probabilities of an item sum to one.

The three profiles differ in media use and in work. At prompts in profile 3, students used social media with probability 0.792, watched TV or played video games with probability 0.397, and listened to music with probability 0.366. In profile 2 the same probabilities are 0.127, 0.159 and 0.083, and time with friends (0.165 against 0.100) and walking (0.144 against 0.091) are somewhat more likely. Both report sports at about 0.07. At prompts in profile 1 students worked at a part-time job with probability 1.000 and reported every other activity with probability below 0.05. Profile 3 is therefore a media-heavy pattern, profile 2 a pattern of little media use with the remaining activities at their usual low rates, and profile 1 a pattern of work with little else.

The response plot draws the same probabilities, one line per profile across the items.

plot_responses(lca)

The media-heavy and low-media lines separate on the three media items and nearly coincide on sports, while the work profile stands apart on the part-time job item.

Two student classes

The "counts" table gives the size of each profile and class, and the "profile_probabilities" table the profile mix of each student class.

get_results(lca, "counts")
#>         level class effective_count effective_proportion
#> 1 individuals     1            91.4               0.0354
#> 2 individuals     2          1848.0               0.7157
#> 3 individuals     3           642.6               0.2489
#> 4      groups     1            43.6               0.4357
#> 5      groups     2            56.4               0.5643
get_results(lca, "profile_probabilities")
#>   group_class profile probability group_class_probability
#> 1           1       1     0.00778                   0.436
#> 2           1       2     0.46348                   0.436
#> 3           1       3     0.52874                   0.436
#> 4           2       1     0.05862                   0.564
#> 5           2       2     0.92787                   0.564
#> 6           2       3     0.01351                   0.564

The low-media profile holds 71.6% of prompts, the media-heavy profile 24.9% and the work profile 3.5%. The student classes differ sharply in their mix. In class 2, which holds 56.4% of students, 0.928 of prompts fall in the low-media profile, 0.059 in the work profile and only 0.014 in the media-heavy one. In class 1, with 43.6% of students, the media-heavy profile is the more common, at 0.529, and the work profile almost absent, at 0.008. Media-heavy leisure is therefore concentrated in a minority of students, and for them it is the usual pattern, while most students almost never report it. Part-time work appears mainly among the students of the low-media class.

The probability plot compares the two mixes.

plot_prevalence(lca)

Class 2 runs close to one on the low-media profile and close to zero on the media-heavy one; class 1 divides its prompts between those two profiles, with the larger share on the media-heavy profile.

Classification certainty

Profiles and classes are estimated as posterior probabilities. Relative entropy summarizes how concentrated those probabilities are, from 0 for no separation to 1 for certain assignment, and the "classification" table reports the average posterior probability of each assigned class.

get_results(lca, "entropy")
#>         level n_classes n_units entropy_sum relative_entropy
#> 1 individuals         3    2582      556.82            0.804
#> 2      groups         2     100        8.48            0.878
get_results(lca, "classification")
#>         level class n_modal proportion_modal estimated_n estimated_proportion average_posterior
#> 1 individuals     1      92           0.0356        91.4               0.0354             0.991
#> 2 individuals     2    1896           0.7343      1848.0               0.7157             0.930
#> 3 individuals     3     594           0.2301       642.6               0.2489             0.858
#> 4      groups     1      42           0.4200        43.6               0.4357             0.971
#> 5      groups     2      58           0.5800        56.4               0.5643             0.952
#>   odds_correct_classification
#> 1                      3110.0
#> 2                         5.3
#> 3                        18.2
#> 4                        43.6
#> 5                        15.3

Relative entropy is 0.804 for prompts and 0.878 for students. A single prompt answers eight yes/no questions, which leaves its profile less certain; a student contributes many prompts, which pins down the class. The average posterior probability is 0.991 for prompts assigned to the work profile, 0.930 for the low-media profile and 0.858 for the media-heavy one, and 0.952 and 0.971 for the two student classes. Conclusions about students are therefore well supported, while an analysis of individual prompts should carry the posterior probabilities forward.

Local independence

The model assumes the items are independent within a profile. The "residuals" table measures the association that each pair of items keeps within a profile, with a chi-square test for each pair; the ten largest are shown.

get_results(lca, "residuals") |> head(10)
#>      profile       indicator_1    indicator_2        kind observed expected residual effective_n
#> 1  profile_1   on_social_media        walking categorical   0.4240 1.60e-16   0.4240        91.4

The largest residual, 0.424, links social media and walking in the work profile, which holds about 91 prompts, so it rests on few observations. Next, in the media-heavy profile, come sports and walking (0.166), friends and walking (0.143) and music and walking (0.133). Physical and social activities occur together more often than three profiles allow, which is one reason BIC rewards larger models: extra profiles can absorb this association.

Uncertainty in the response probabilities

parameter_inference() gives standard errors and 95% Wald intervals for every parameter. Several response probabilities lie on their bound: the work profile reports TV or games, music and sports with probability zero and a part-time job with probability one, and the low-media profile reports a part-time job with probability zero. Wald inference does not apply at a bound, so boundary = "fix" holds these probabilities at their values, leaves them out of the table and reports the other parameters conditionally on them. The intervals of the “yes” probabilities, in the rows whose term ends in :yes, show how firmly the profiles are distinguished.

parameter_inference(lca, boundary = "fix")
#>          level       outcome                  term   parameter estimate standard_error statistic
#> 1  measurement     profile_1  time_with_friends:no    response  0.97814        0.01531        NA
#> 2  measurement     profile_1 time_with_friends:yes    response  0.02186        0.01531        NA
#> 3  measurement     profile_2  time_with_friends:no    response  0.83512        0.00972        NA
#> 4  measurement     profile_2 time_with_friends:yes    response  0.16488        0.00972        NA
#> 5  measurement     profile_3  time_with_friends:no    response  0.89992        0.01522        NA
#> 6  measurement     profile_3 time_with_friends:yes    response  0.10008        0.01522        NA
#> 7  measurement     profile_1    on_social_media:no    response  0.98866        0.01353        NA
#> 8  measurement     profile_1   on_social_media:yes    response  0.01134        0.01353        NA

The profiles are clearly separated on the media items: the interval for social media is 0.715 to 0.853 in the media-heavy profile and 0.094 to 0.170 in the low-media profile. On sports the two intervals overlap almost entirely. The part-time job probability in the media-heavy profile has an interval of 0.010 to 0.033, close to zero, because very few of its prompts report a job.

Adding affect

A mixed model adds three affect ratings (happy, relaxed, exhausted, each from 1 to 7) as continuous indicators. worried is left out because about half of its ratings are 1, which can push a profile’s variance to its lower bound. The same happens to exhausted with three profiles: one profile collects the prompts rated 1 and its variance reaches the bound, so the mixed model is fitted with two profiles and two classes.

mixed <- multilpa(student_esm,
                  vars = c("happy", "relaxed", "exhausted", activities),
                  categorical = activities, id = "student", n_profiles = 2,
                  n_group_classes = 2, n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
get_results(mixed)

With affect included, the profiles become profiles of mood. Profile 1 has mean ratings of 5.85 for happy, 5.59 for relaxed and 2.55 for exhausted; profile 2 has 3.59, 3.33 and 4.33. The activities now differ less and in a different way: time with friends is reported at 0.188 of profile-1 prompts and 0.084 of profile-2 prompts, social media at 0.269 and 0.315. Good mood goes with social time more than with media use. The student classes remain distinct: 0.874 of the prompts of class 1 fall in the low-mood profile, and 0.833 of those of class 2 in the good-mood profile. The profiles a model finds are set by the indicators it is given, so the choice of indicators is part of the question.

Interpretation

Students’ leisure at non-study prompts falls into three patterns: one defined by social media, TV and music, one with little media use, and a small one of part-time work with little else. The distinction that matters most is between students: a majority almost never reports the media-heavy pattern, and a minority reports it at more than half of their prompts. Part-time work appears mainly among the majority. That student-level result is well supported by the classification diagnostics, while the assignment of any single prompt is less certain.

Limitations

The data contain only prompts at which the student had not studied, so the patterns describe leisure time, not the whole day. The three-profile model leaves association between physical and social activities within its profiles, and larger models fit better by BIC but are not stable across starts on these data. The choice of three profiles itself depends on enough starts: with few, the model stops at a lower maximum and two profiles are chosen. Prompts are treated as independent given the student’s class, so the model ignores the order of prompts within a day. The associations are observational and say nothing about causes.

Reference

Neubauer, A. B., & Schmiedek, F. (2024). Approaching academic adjustment on multiple time scales. Zeitschrift für Erziehungswissenschaft, 27(1), 147-168. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11618-023-01182-8
